Citizen Lab says it believes **dozens of devices** at Al Jazeera were compromised by spyware delivered through Discover-Tech ads. Discover-Tech’s **Controlium** software can profile users, then let clients **covertly hack** selected targets with third-party spyware.

cards.title: I Know Why the Mathematicians Weep

depth.text: an essay asks why **mathematicians are grieving** as AI produces proofs that **stumped experts for decades**

OpenAI has published **hundreds of math findings**, including proofs that stumped top mathematicians for decades or centuries. The essay argues the work advances mathematics’ craft but interrupts its **human conversation**, raising the fear of **knowledge without understanding**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see AI as a threat to mathematicians’ purpose, status, and livelihoods; others say it will push the field’s frontier and leave room for human mathematics.
entities: Making It Explicit: Reasoning, Representing, and Discursive Commitment

comments.text: I think beyond the specific elements of any domain AI eclipses humans in, overall, the notion of the thing that grants you status, prestige, and a living wage being commodified would spark in anyone a profound sense of dread. Beyond just making you redundant in your job, the whole architecture of your existence, the thousands of hours of struggle, the sacrifice of putting off social games or…

This piece circles, without naming it, around the concept of “deontic scorekeeping” central to the work of Robert Brandom on semantics. The idea that our ability to create and sustain conceptual systems depends on the give and take of reasons within a social setting. Brandom has been front of mind for me lately because elements of his theory both explain why LLMs should work in principle, and…

I think Thompson has no understanding of endeavors like pure math or the theoretical sciences. In the words of Einstein, "I want to know how God created this world. I am not interested in this or that phenomenon, in the spectrum of this or that element. I want to know his thoughts; the rest [is] just details." I think mathematicians aren't bemoaning their lost sunk costs. They're now aware that…

I still think mathematicians are going to be as important as ever. The LLMs are only finding what was technically possible given our current breadth of knowledge after brute force solving problems. Eventually it will run out of things that it can do with its training and the only way to get it to do more will be training it on new human found knowledge. Finding that new knowledge may be…

Article refers to Hugo Duminil-Copin, who also did a podcast with Brady Haran [1] about this subject, for him it isn't case of bruised ego, or gatekeeping. He realized that the way things were done were going to change, and it made him emotional, he is not pessimistic or against AI. [1]: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=omuJpoV-Ko4

cards.title: It took me nine years to hack my Xbox 360

depth.text: someone finally **hacked an Xbox 360** after nine years, with help from a **cheap microcontroller**

The trick was **fault injection**: researchers glitched an instruction in the Xbox 360’s signature check so it ignored a value it was meant to move. A **Raspberry Pi Pico** made the console storage dump take only a handful of seconds. Then a software-only Xbox 360 exploit **dropped just last week**, making the hardware effort feel a bit moot.

cards.camps: Two camps: the post says cheap microcontrollers made fault-injection work more accessible; MayeulC says similar hardware capability was already quite cheap in 2017 and before.

comments.text: This blogpost makes the point that the advent of the Raspberry Pi microcontroller made it easier to interface with a variety of hardware. And it is true, but the capability was already quite cheap in 2017 and before: fx2 chips can do quite a lot, for instance. I hope Bunnie's Baochip BIO approach will take off in microcontrollers, making that sort of feature more ubiquitous. You can do a lot of…

What did Microslop change in Xbox One that prevented it from being exploited much in the same way? Afaik Xbone is still undefeated in terms of security, either because it's so good or because it's just uninteresting console to own

This talk was linked in a comment that was just flagged for unrelated reasons but I wanted to post this talk in case anyone missed it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U7VwtOrwceo It is an excellent talk into why the security of the Xbox is so good by the platform security architect himself(at least the software stack). I highly recommend a watch.

Tangential history: to this day there's still DNA of the Xenos GPU from the XBox 360 inside every Snapdragon GPU (Adreno). Way back around 2008, AMD was bleeding money after its acquisition of ATI. They wanted to divest of their Handheld division, which was the business unit that was producing chips for smartphones. From what I heard through the grapevine, Qualcomm was interested only in some…
And now we have a working permanent softmod. The Xbox 360 hacking scene is basically complete at this point.

cards.title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke

The author says Scion’s **“derived data”** resembles Mononoke, which they helped build at Meta; they say Anthropic credited Sapling but **left Mononoke unmentioned**. cards.title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years

depth.text: Americans report doing **less** of many **social activities**, from entertaining at home to going to church

Data for Progress compared a 2026 survey of 1,098 U.S. adults with a 1995 survey: home entertaining fell from **88% to 67%**, and church attendance from 74% to 54%. The surveys used **different methods**, so the authors say the results suggest trends, not a precise estimate of change.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters blame screens and online entertainment; others point to costs, housing, work and family schedules, and social spaces designed for isolation.

Another reason I might posit is declining birth rates and an…

cards.title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?

depth.text: someone argues rationalist bloggers **write too much** instead of questioning their **starting assumptions**

Alex Wennerberg says he cut around **70%** of his draft; his piece was 2,700 words, after he skimmed Scott Alexander’s **25,000-word post**. He argues **verbosity** can stand in for thoroughness, while the community prizes unconventional ideas over common sense and tradition.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say rationalist writing is bloated and tedious; defenders say detail and nuance matter, and argue the author dismisses careful arguments too easily.

comments.text: > adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating the one or two assumptions they make at the start or broadening their philosophical background beyond the collection of texts popular within their subculture. Personally i think the world would be a better place if more of us added nuance to our arguments.

> Eliezer Yudkowsky's "sequences" are over one million words long. This is a particularly weird example. The median post in the "sequences" is less than 1000 words long. The sequences are mostly a long series of individually very short blogposts.

The Economist is so good in this respect. A smart, very good writer will write something and get to the point quickly. Articles are mostly a page or less. Writing like that respects people's time. Many bloggers could do with writing things more briefly. The author of this piece also makes a very good point that often long pieces go into weird corners of their own argument without thinking about…

"The idea that something may be true, valuable, or good merely because it is common sense or inherited tradition is anathema to them" This is reasonable though. Tradition and common sense suggest value perhaps more than rationalists think, but if tradition and common sense have value, there is an underlying reason.

Agree with the author. Most rationalist material I've tried to read it's incredibly lengthy and frequently boring. It's also true that they are using verbosity and a certain academic style to hide the lack of precision and correctness. They are prolific writers, but not great.

cards.title: Tiny Little Office

depth.text: someone made a **free office suite** in one website, with documents stored in the link
One commenter says Claude can read the site's **llms.txt** and generate **URLs that render documents**. Others asked about opening saved files and adding **PDF annotation**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise it; others want desktop apps or say the functionality has been available for decades.

comments.text: As a kid in the late 1980s, my dad got me a PC (an Olivetti IBM clone to be precise). I distinctly remember that there were separate apps for spreadsheets (Lotus 1-2-3 [0]), charts (Harvard Graphics [1]) and word processing (Chi Writer [2]). It has a much larger featureset but is specifically focused on presentations (for now!). Unlike this project, the editor and content embed themselves in an html file, so you aren't dependent on the host site existing to serve the editor.

Tell Claude or whatever to read https://tinylittleoffice.com/llms.txt and it will then be able to generate URLs that render documents. Here's a deck I had it generate about how the URL format works: https://bit.ly/4yRBc1v

I'm intrigued about the "Trip Planner" being a top-level app. Only tried it in a very surface level way, but the recent trips I've planned (Ottawa for 6 people, Cancun for ~20) have ended up as an ugly mishmash of spreadsheets + google maps saved locations list + random chatgpt sessions. It feels like there's an unmet need there for managing something more flexible than a minute by minute…

cards.title: Yandex outage: data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots moved

depth.text: Cloudflare found **malicious bots** **moved to other hosts** instead of stopping

Bot requests from Yandex.Cloud to one gambling account **dropped to zero**, but **identical requests** soon appeared from Radist and Selectel. Russian bot traffic to gambling accounts stayed essentially flat: 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%).

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say bots moved rather than stopped; others point to steep traffic drops and possible downstream effects from losing Yandex services.

cards.title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers

depth.text: Jev is letting people try **image support**, **bounding boxes**, and **longer context** as experimental features

comments.text: > Warning: AI benchmarks. Please don't trust them I like that they're being up front about this. Benchmarks are a metric that can be gamed. They give you an approximate estimate of where things land, but you really need to test for your use case.

In case you need something a bit more lightweight, or want privacy. You can get amazing (better in a lot of cases) accuracy and performance from local models that run and train on CPU: https://jeffyclassify.com/blog/when-llms-fail-at-classificat...

If you're looking for a decent local model, JevK5-4B is excellent. On my own benchmark for the things I work with (seeing if the answer to a question was correct given the evidence that was provided), it was within a point of jev.

cards.title: America didn't lose its rare earth industry, it sold it

depth.text: the US **sold its rare earth industry**, and the authors pitch a **plan to rebuild it**

The authors propose a **CoCo bond**: it pays interest in quiet years, **shares cash flow** after the producer hits a capacity threshold, and can **convert into equity** if both triggers fire. One trigger is reaching a defined capacity target; the other is a sustained breach of an agreed price band or an externally observed exercise of the chokepoint.
data: China's share of world rare earth refining
China's share of heavy rare earth refining
loan authority earmarked for critical minerals
convertible preferred stock in the MP Materials deal

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say production moved because market costs made it rational; others want government intervention, with one proposing a federal company instead of the authors’ financing plan.

cards.title: Starlink limit hits Ukraine's drones

depth.text: a new **speed limit** from SpaceX may be disrupting **Ukraine's drone missions**

Initial reports put the threshold at **around 160 km/h**; later reports said some operators lost communication at **60–70 km/h**, though that lower figure is unconfirmed. The service carries commands, video and mission updates, and SpaceX has not confirmed a **political motive**.

comments.text: The timing is interesting, given that it comes days after Musk said Ukraine had gone "too far" striking Yandex data centers. Putting other considerations aside, these strikes could be interpreted as direct retaliation against strikes on Ukrainian data centers days before. That said, depending on a single piece of tech is not a good idea (as evidenced by the Russians when they lost starlink…

cards.title: Why do LLM pelicans look like this?

depth.text: someone says **AI pelicans** keep coming out **alike**, even when a simple prompt leaves room for variety

The post compares SVGs from the same pelican-and-bicycle prompt and calls the similar results **“diversity collapse.”** Its UI-design benchmark puts the best model at **65.5**, against **92.3** for a human reference.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say a plain prompt should get a plain pelican and variation should be requested; others say the repeated compositions point to a real lack of model diversity.

comments.text: I'm not clear on what the claim is here. The article faults LLMs for not being more creative (riding in the city in the rain, in East Asia, in outer space, etc.). But, if prompted, "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle," with no additional details or specification, then I would _expect_ something generic: a side view, nondescript terrain or perhaps terrain associated with a pelican…

The lack of variety is probably the most underrated issue, and the most likely cause of annoying patterns you all hate. All current post-trained LLMs are mode-collapsed compared to the post-training set distribution, and this doesn't get nearly enough attention from the labs and independent researchers. It's far from being a transformer-only problem, it's a common failure mode in all kinds of…

The example just doesn't support the claim. If I ask for a pelican riding a bicycle, I am expecting a relatively boring image of a pelican riding a bicycle, not a pelican flying through a thunderstorm while on a bicycle. That's just straight up not what I asked for. I didn't ask it to be creative, when I imagine myself riding a bicycle, I'm not flying! If I added "be creative and unique, you can…

It is fairly easy to go ask for a differently styled pelican, environment, background, etc. But that's not the point. I was thinking just today about how, if I could hire my competition's lead designer/programmers, have them design a system for me cleanroom, that I'd effectively know everything there is to know about my competition's limitations. This is trivial to do with LLMs. "Make me a thing…
A good prompt will shift the distribution away from average eg: https://john.hartnup.uk/2026/06/07/ai-event-posters.html This is a feature, not a bug.
